subject: English
chapter_title: The Day the River Spoke (Learning Together)
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read — pre-reading I (p.1): listen to surroundings, share observations aloud.
Let us read — pre-reading II (p.1): predict Jahnavi's dream and how she might achieve it.

periods.activity_title: Opening the Story: Who Is Jahnavi?
materials: Textbook — The Day the River Spoke (p.1–2)

time_bands.activity: Students close their eyes and quietly listen to sounds around them for a brief stretch. Each student shares one sound heard and whether it seemed to carry a message — a quick paired exchange before the class opens the story.

Teacher reads aloud the brief character introduction of Jahnavi on page 1, with students following. The class hears that she is a bright girl in a coastal village whose parents farm and who minds younger siblings.

Pre-reading II: teacher places Jahnavi's situation before the class — a girl with a dream — and invites open responses: what might her dream be and what might she do to make it real? Students speak in turns; teacher gathers ideas on the board without endorsing any, leaving the story to answer.

Brief whole-class share of personal dreams — one sentence each from three or four volunteers. Teacher links the variety of responses to the story ahead, then invites students to keep their predictions in mind as they read.

periods.teacher_notes: Jahnavi is a girl kept home to mind siblings while her brother Gopi attends school — establishing this detail clearly now gives students the emotional anchor the story depends on. A common pitfall is letting the discussion drift into generic talk of 'dreams' without tying it back to Jahnavi's specific, constrained situation. Students who have not contributed orally may be invited to write one word on a slip of paper as their prediction.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss — after Section I (p.3): Jahnavi's dream and whether the River can help her.

periods.activity_title: The River Stirs: Reading Section I Aloud
materials: Textbook — The Day the River Spoke (p.1–3)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Section I of the prose aloud (pages 1–3), students following in their books. The reading covers Jahnavi sitting by the river, the kingfisher, the lizard, her silent weeping, and the River's first murmuring words — an unhurried reading aloud that lets the natural descriptions and the River's voice register fully.

Comprehension discussion on the two post-reading questions: what Jahnavi's dream is and why it matters to her, and whether the River can genuinely help her fulfill it. Students respond in turn; teacher steers toward textual evidence, asking students to point to the page where Jahnavi's longing is shown.

Teacher draws attention to the natural imagery — kingfisher, lizard, rustling bamboo — and asks students to say in a single sentence why the writer sets the scene this way before the River speaks. Two or three responses are heard, then the teacher holds the question open for later reflection.

periods.teacher_notes: Having introduced Jahnavi's situation and her desire to go to school, this reading gives students the story's emotional core. A common pitfall is reading too quickly past the nature descriptions; the prose_summary notes that these are central to the story's appeal, so linger on them and invite students to visualise the scene. Students uncertain about the River as a character may be guided to notice that the story explicitly marks the voice as the River's.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss — after Section II (p.6): complete table of Jahnavi's questions and River's answers.

periods.activity_title: Jahnavi and the River Converse: Reading Section II
materials: Textbook — The Day the River Spoke (p.3–6)

time_bands.activity: Shared reading of Section II (pages 3–6): teacher and students alternate paragraphs, with the teacher modelling the River's sleepy, witty voice and inviting volunteers to voice Jahnavi's lines. The reading covers Jahnavi's curious questions — yellow spiders, bamboo, moon, frogs — and the River's gentle, encouraging responses.

Students work in pairs to complete the two-column table matching Jahnavi's questions (Column 1) to the River's answers (Column 2), using pages 3–6. Teacher circulates, prompting students to locate each answer in the text rather than guess. Pairs compare answers with the adjacent pair before a whole-class check.

Teacher highlights the River's reply that little girls can do as much as little boys, asks students to respond in one sentence: does the River's argument convince them? A quick paired exchange closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The dialogue between Jahnavi and the River carries the story's central argument on gender equality — the prose_summary notes the River reminds her that 'little girls can do as much as little boys'. A common pitfall in table-completion tasks is students copying the first phrase they find; prompt them to check that the answer column actually responds to the question column. The exchange about ships at the end of Section II is a natural curiosity hook worth noting aloud.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — Extract 1 (p.7): tone, frequent-visitor phrase, punctuation effect, River's qualities.
Let us think and reflect — Extract 2 (p.7–8): fill reason for equality, true/false encouragement, meaning of 'slip along', repetition of 'I couldn't'.

materials: Textbook — The Day the River Spoke (p.7–8)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 1 aloud ('You shouldn't cry, you know…I've got to hurry to reach the sea, you know') as students follow on page 7. A brief pause: students identify the speaker and the listener before any questions are set.

Students work individually on the four Extract 1 questions on page 7: identifying the River's tone, selecting the phrase showing Jahnavi is a regular visitor, interpreting the exclamation mark, and choosing three qualities of the River from the word box. Teacher takes responses question by question, inviting students to cite the extract.

Extract 2 ('Can I do something?…They'd chase me out') is read by a volunteer. Students tackle the four questions on pages 7–8 — the reason girls and boys are equal, whether the statement about the River's encouragement is true or false, the meaning of 'slip along', and what the repeated 'I couldn't' reveals. Responses are heard and discussed briefly for each question.

Teacher draws the two extracts together: the River moves from comforting Jahnavi (Extract 1) to pushing her toward action (Extract 2). Students name this shift in one word; the best word is noted on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the dialogue between Jahnavi and the River across Sections I and II, students are now equipped to read the extracts analytically. The prose_summary notes that Jahnavi's repeated 'I couldn't' reflects her deep fear of being turned away — draw students toward this emotional layer rather than a surface grammar reading. Students may confuse 'tone' with 'mood'; clarify that tone describes the speaker's attitude, not the reader's feeling.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — II (p.8): nature's role, River's knowledge, Jahnavi's age-fear, River's laughter, River's advice, conversation's appeal, writer's message.

periods.activity_title: Deeper Questions: Reflecting on Story and Theme
materials: Textbook — The Day the River Spoke (p.8–15)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the final section of the prose (pages 8–15) in summary, touching on Jahnavi slipping into school, the teacher's visit to her father, her mother's support, and Jahnavi's resolve to become a teacher. This reading aloud — brief and scene-setting — ensures all students have heard the story's conclusion before the reflective questions.

Class discusses six of the seven reflective questions on page 8 in sequence: why the writer describes nature in detail at the opening; how the River knew so much about Jahnavi; what Jahnavi's line 'I'm so old now' reveals; why the River laughed; and why Jahnavi should follow the River's advice. Teacher invites one response per question, encourages disagreement, and uses the prose_summary to arbitrate when answers diverge.

The final extended question — the main message the writer intends to convey — is treated as a short individual writing task: each student writes two sentences in their notebook. Three responses are read aloud; teacher synthesises the themes of education, gender equality, and courage without prescribing a single 'correct' answer.

periods.teacher_notes: The prose_summary identifies the central themes as the right to education, gender equality, self-belief, and the power of nature as witness and counsel — keep responses anchored to these four. A common pitfall is students treating the 'message' question as a moral-of-the-story exercise with a single sentence; encourage them to hold two or three ideas together. Students who have not yet followed the story's ending can be directed to the prose's final scene where Jahnavi runs to the river to share her triumph.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen — I (p.39): circle words used by the five speakers from the word box as you listen.
Let us listen — II (p.12): match seven statements to the correct speaker after second listening.

periods.activity_title: Five Voices on School: Listening and Matching
materials: Transcript text (p.39) — teacher's copy for reading aloud

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the five speakers — Father, Grandmother, Teacher, Student, Principal — and displays the ten words from the word box on the board. Students are briefed: they will circle the words they hear as the transcript is read aloud; two words are not used.

Teacher reads the transcript aloud at a measured pace, each speaker distinctly voiced. Students circle words from the box; no writing of answers yet. After the first reading, students compare their circled words briefly with a neighbour.

Teacher reads the transcript a second time. Students now focus on the seven statements on page 12 — which speaker said what. They write the speaker number against each statement on their own copy, knowing two statements are not needed.

Whole-class check: teacher reads each statement aloud; students call out the speaker number; teacher confirms or corrects with a line from the transcript. Discussion: which speaker's view was most surprising or most convincing, and why — a quick paired exchange before the class closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The listening transcript features five distinct perspectives on schooling from Father, Grandmother, Teacher, Student, and Principal — ensuring students link each viewpoint to the right speaker is the core challenge, not just the vocabulary recognition. A common pitfall is students confusing Statement 7 (learning skills is not gender-based — Teacher) with Statement 3 (education leads to freedom of choice — Father); read those two statements side by side during the check. The two unused statements should be identified explicitly so students understand the exercise's design.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak — I (p.13): read the River's sentence in varied voices (happy, angry, sad, worried, etc.).
Let us speak — II (p.13): paired advice-giving across four real-life situations, roles reversed.

periods.activity_title: Asking for and Giving Advice: Paired Role-Play

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the River's sentence ('Dear, dear! What's the matter?…') in a sleepy voice, then models a second reading in a worried voice. Pairs are formed; each pair chooses two different voices from the hint list and reads the sentence aloud in each, paying attention to pace and stress. Two pairs perform for the class; the class names the voice they heard.

Speaking task II: teacher reads all four situations aloud and models the advice-asking and advice-giving exchange for Situation (i) — joining an all-boys football team. Pairs then work through Situations (ii), (iii), and (iv) in sequence, swapping roles after each situation. Teacher circulates, listening for complete sentences and encouraging students to give a reason with their advice, as the River does in the story.

Two pairs share their exchange for one situation of their choice. Class gives brief feedback: was the advice clear? Was a reason given? Teacher connects this to how the River gave Jahnavi concrete, reasoned advice rather than vague encouragement.

periods.teacher_notes: Having followed the River's advice-giving conversation with Jahnavi, students are now practising the same speech act in new, familiar contexts. A common pitfall is students giving one-word advice ('just do it'); prompt them to use the River's pattern — acknowledge the problem, state the advice, give a reason. Students who are hesitant to speak aloud can be paired with a supportive partner and given the first turn as advice-seeker rather than giver.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — Observing Nature (p.14): plan and draft a titled descriptive paragraph on a nature observation, using the prompts table.

periods.activity_title: Observing Nature: Planning and Writing a Descriptive Paragraph

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the observation habit using the story's opening: Jahnavi notices the kingfisher swooping, the lizard basking, the river's sound. Students spend a brief stretch looking out a window or recalling a recent outdoor moment and jotting three details — a colour, a texture, a movement — in their notebooks.

Teacher displays the six prompts from the Ideas table ('Every day, I see… / I find it very interesting that… / I like… because… / I feel… as… / I want to tell you that… / My advice to all is…') and models one paragraph sentence per prompt orally. Students choose a title for their paragraph and write it at the top of a fresh page.

Students write their descriptive paragraph independently, aiming for five to seven sentences that move through at least four of the six prompts. Teacher circulates, offering brief individual guidance on word choice — encouraging sensory language (colour, sound, texture) rather than summary statements. Students who finish early are asked to re-read and replace one generic word with a more precise one.

Two or three volunteers read their paragraphs aloud. Class listens and names one vivid detail they found striking. Teacher collects notebooks; written pieces are returned with a brief written comment.

periods.teacher_notes: The story's richly described natural setting — kingfisher, lizard, rustling bamboo, the river's sounds — gives students a ready model of observation-based writing. A common pitfall is students writing a list of facts rather than a descriptive paragraph; the prompts 'I feel… as…' and 'I find it very interesting that…' are the ones most likely to generate genuine descriptive language and should be highlighted. The paragraph is planned, drafted, peer-shared, and collected in a single unit so no continuation is needed.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — I (p.8): why 'River' is capitalised — personification and proper-noun logic.
Let us learn — II (p.8–9): match nine sound-word definitions to words from the text; fill blanks in classroom scene.

periods.activity_title: Words That Sound: Personification, Sound Words, and Loanwords

time_bands.activity: Teacher places the question on the board: why is the word 'River' written with a capital letter in the story when it is a common noun? Students discuss briefly in pairs, then respond. Teacher guides them toward personification — the River speaks, consoles, laughs, and advises, making it a character with human qualities, hence treated as a proper noun in the story.

Students open to the sound-word matching table on page 8. Teacher reads each definition aloud; students predict the word and locate it in the text before writing. After the nine matches are completed, students tackle the fill-in exercise on page 9, using the matched words to complete the classroom-scene passage. Answers are checked whole-class, with teacher reading the completed passage fluently.

Teacher introduces the loanword idea using 'catamaran' from the text — from Tamil 'kattu maram', tied wood. Students hear the list of eight loanwords (karma, sahib, chutney, guru, verandah, jungle, areca, palanquin) and, as a class, guess which Indian language two or three of them might come from. The full research task is set as homework, with students directed to page 9 for the full list.

periods.teacher_notes: The sound-word matching task is grounded in words the text itself uses — screech, splash, murmur, sob, rustle, gasp, rattle, noisy, wail — so students should be directed to re-read the opening paragraphs of the story to locate each word in context before choosing. A common pitfall is students completing the fill-in exercise by guessing from the word shape rather than meaning; insist on reading the whole sentence before filling the blank. The loanword homework is a self-study pointer for students who wish to extend their exploration of Indian languages.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn — III (p.9): find meanings and Indian-language origins of eight loanwords (karma, sahib, chutney, etc.).

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — VI (p.11): fill six blanks with correct prepositions in Jahnavi's first school day passage.
Let us learn — VII (p.11–12): fill eight blanks distinguishing prepositions from adverbs (on, off, up, down, etc.).

periods.activity_title: Prepositions, Adverbs, and Water Transport Words

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes a short sentence on the board — 'Jahnavi stood _____ the gate' — and asks students to supply a word. Three or four options are heard; teacher uses them to define preposition as a word showing direction, location, time, or relationship, and distinguishes it from adverb use of the same word ('she ran outside').

Students work individually on the preposition fill-in task on page 11 — Jahnavi's first day at school. Each blank has bracketed options (at/in/on, etc.); students select and write. Teacher then reads the completed passage aloud with the correct answers, asking students to call out the preposition before each blank is filled.

Task VII on pages 11–12: eight sentences using on, off, up, down as either preposition or adverb. Teacher models the first two by asking 'does the word show a relationship between two nouns, or does it just describe the action?' Students complete the remaining six. Whole-class check: students name the function (preposition or adverb) before the answer is confirmed.

Teacher closes with the crossword on page 10 — water transport vocabulary. Students hear five clues read aloud and call out answers as a warm-end word game. The crossword itself is noted as a self-study activity for students who want to complete it independently.

periods.teacher_notes: The preposition fill-in passage on page 11 uses the story's own character and event — Jahnavi's first school day — which links grammar practice to the prose students have already read. A common pitfall is students choosing prepositions by sound ('it feels right') rather than function; the bracket options are a deliberate scaffold, so ensure students read all options before choosing. Tasks IV and V (boat drawings and crossword) are self-study pointers for students who wish to explore the water transport vocabulary further.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore — III (p.15): read the poster 'The Happiness of a Nation lies in the Dignity of its Daughters' and answer four questions.
Let us explore — II (p.14): class survey of languages spoken; brief oral share of preferred reading language.

periods.activity_title: Rivers, Languages, and the Rights of Girls

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a brief whole-class survey: how many languages can each student speak? Students call out; teacher records on the board in a simple tally. The class counts the total and discusses in one or two sentences why India's multilingual character is something to value — linking to the story's theme of learning as a right for all.

Teacher reads the poster text aloud: 'The Happiness of a Nation lies in the Dignity of its Daughters.' Students work individually to answer the four questions on page 15 — what they observe in the poster, why the girls look happy, the relationship between dignity and happiness, and how a nation prospers when its daughters are happy. After individual writing, three students share their answers to the extended questions.

Teacher introduces Beyond-text task I on page 14: why are India's rivers often considered sacred and referred to as female? Students discuss in small groups for a brief stretch, drawing on geography, culture, and the story itself — the River as a wise, maternal voice. Two groups share their reasoning; teacher adds the example of the Brahmaputra and Sone as male rivers.

Homework task IV on page 15 is introduced: students research two additional government schemes for the education of the girl child. Teacher names the three schemes mentioned in the textbook and asks students to note them as a starting point.

periods.teacher_notes: The poster task on page 15 connects the story's theme of girls' education to a public-health message, requiring students to read a visual text alongside verbal text — a functional reading move that extends beyond the prose. A common pitfall is students listing what they see in the poster (two girls, a school building) without connecting the image to the slogan's argument; push them toward the relationship between dignity and happiness as the question demands. Beyond-text task I on discussing sacred rivers can generate rich discussion but should stay time-bounded.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore — IV (p.15): research two additional government schemes for girl child education and note them for sharing.

items.item_stem: Read the following statement and choose the correct answer. Jahnavi weeps silently by the river because she has been kept at home to care for her siblings while her brother Gopi attends school, and she is frightened it is already too late for her to go. Which of the following best describes her feeling at this point in the story?

options.label: A
options.text: A longing for school held back by fear of having missed her chance.

options.label: B
options.text: Anger at her parents for making an unfair rule.

options.label: C
options.text: Contentment with her life by the river, disturbed by a strange voice.

options.label: D
options.text: Jealousy of her neighbour Meena's ability to make friends at school.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests the student focuses on injustice in general rather than Jahnavi's specific emotional state, which is fear rather than anger.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misreads the opening scene — Jahnavi weeps because she cannot attend school, not because the river's voice disturbs her peace.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a character detail not central to this moment; Meena is a schoolmate of Gopi, not the object of Jahnavi's longing.

items.source_lo: Student reads a prose narrative with attention to character motivation, narrative voice, and authorial choices, using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Jahnavi's desire for schooling, River's personification, gender-equality argument, nature imagery, story's central themes.
items.item_stem: The writer describes the kingfisher swooping, the lizard basking, and the murmuring river before Jahnavi speaks a single word. Why do you think the writer chooses to open the story with these details of nature? What effect does this choice have on how we understand Jahnavi's situation? Write your answer in two or three sentences.

expected_elements: Nature is alive and observing, mirroring the River's role as a silent witness.
The peaceful scene contrasts with Jahnavi's inner sorrow, deepening the reader's empathy.
Establishing nature as attentive prepares the reader for the River speaking.
Any two of the above points expressed in the student's own words are sufficient.

items.source_context: Five speakers — Father, Grandmother, Teacher, Student, Principal — share views on schooling and gender equality in education.
items.item_stem: Listen to the transcript of five speakers sharing their views on school. After listening, decide whether each of the following statements is True or False based on what the speakers said.

options.text: The Father believes that whether his daughter works outside or stays at home should be her own choice.
The Grandmother says that all girls in her time were able to attend school freely.
The Student says she enjoys school mainly because she wins prizes in competitions.
The Teacher says that school prepares students by developing respect for head, hands, and heart.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — The Father says whether his daughter wants to work in an organisation or be a homemaker, it should be her choice.
2. False — The Grandmother says many girls in her time could not attend school because some village elders felt girls should help at home.
3. True — The Teacher mentions developing respect for head, hands and heart as part of what school prepares students for.
4. False — The Student says she likes school because she reads books and learns about the world, and has friends to share her feelings with.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a multi-speaker passage and identifies specific information, distinguishing viewpoints, using listening as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Five speakers — Father, Grandmother, Teacher, Student, Principal — share views on schooling and gender equality in education.
items.item_stem: Among the five speakers in the listening transcript — Father, Grandmother, Teacher, Student, and Principal — two speakers address the idea that education should not be limited by gender. Identify these two speakers and briefly explain, in one sentence each, what each one says about gender and education.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The Father says that education gives freedom of choice, and his daughter should decide her own path — the same as his son. The Teacher says that learning hands-on skills and understanding vocational choices is not gender-based.

items.item_stem: Imagine you are Jahnavi's friend and she comes to you worried, saying she is afraid to enter the classroom on her first day because she thinks the teacher will ask her to leave. Describe the scene: what does Jahnavi say to you, and what advice do you give her? Speak for about one minute. Make sure your advice includes a clear reason, the way the River gave Jahnavi a reason in the story.

expected_elements: Student takes on the role of Jahnavi's friend clearly.
Advice is specific and includes at least one reason.
Speaks in complete sentences with appropriate pace.
Tone is encouraging, matching the River's manner in the story.

items.source_lo: Student uses spoken language to ask for and give advice in a paired exchange, adapting tone to situation, using role-play as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Paired advice-giving modelled on Jahnavi and River's dialogue; four real-life situations involving school and fairness.
items.item_stem: In the story, Jahnavi's mother says she herself once longed for school but was denied by her own mother. Imagine the River could speak to Jahnavi's mother when she was a child, just as it spoke to Jahnavi. What would the River say, and why? Give your opinion with reasons in a spoken response of about one minute. You may agree or disagree with whether the River's advice would have worked for the mother.

expected_elements: Student takes a clear position (agree or disagree) and states it.
Opinion is supported by at least one reason linked to the story.
Refers to the mother's context — a different generation, a different barrier.
Uses appropriate register for expressing an opinion with reasoning.

items.item_stem: The story opens with Jahnavi sitting by a river where she notices a kingfisher swooping, a lizard basking, and the water murmuring. Think of a place in nature that you have visited or can see from where you live. Write a short descriptive paragraph of four to five sentences about that place, focusing on at least two of the following: a colour, a texture, a movement, or a sound you would find there. Give your paragraph a title.

expected_elements: A clear title is given that reflects the observed place.
At least two sensory details (colour, texture, movement, or sound) are present.
Sentences are descriptive, not a list of facts.
Writing is in paragraph form with a logical flow.

items.source_lo: Student writes a descriptive paragraph based on personal observation of nature, selecting precise sensory details, using guided writing as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Descriptive paragraph on nature observations — colours, textures, movements — modelled on the story's opening nature scene.
items.item_stem: At the end of the story, Jahnavi runs back to the river to share her triumph and hears it chuckle. Imagine you are Jahnavi at that moment. Write a paragraph of five to six sentences describing what you see, hear, and feel as you stand by the river after your first day at school. Your paragraph should bring the scene alive through precise sensory details — do not simply tell the reader you are happy. Give your paragraph a title.

At least three sensory details (sight, sound, touch, or emotion-as-sensation) are woven into the description.
Writing shows rather than tells — avoids sentences like 'I was happy'.
The river as a character or presence is reflected in the description.
Paragraph form is maintained; sentences connect logically.

items.item_stem: In the story, the word 'River' is written with a capital letter even though it is a common noun. The story also uses the word 'on' in two different ways — as a preposition and as an adverb. Read these two sentences: (1) Jahnavi placed sleeping Appu on her shoulder. (2) She walked on, quietly, until she reached the school gate. In sentence (1), the word 'on' (in 'on her shoulder') is a preposition. In sentence (2), the word 'on' (in 'walked on') is an adverb. Explain in two sentences why 'River' is capitalised in the story, and then write one sentence of your own using 'down' as an adverb.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The River is capitalised because the author has personified it — given it human qualities like speaking, laughing, and giving advice — so it functions as a character with a name rather than just a body of water. An acceptable adverb sentence would be one where 'down' modifies a verb without linking to a noun, such as 'Jahnavi sat down and began to cry.'

items.item_stem: The poster discussed in the chapter carries the message: 'The Happiness of a Nation lies in the Dignity of its Daughters.' Using what you have understood from the story of Jahnavi and from the poster, write a paragraph of five to six sentences explaining how a nation benefits when its daughters are educated and treated with dignity. You may use examples from the story or from real life.

expected_elements: Connects the poster's message to Jahnavi's story specifically.
Names at least one benefit to society when girls are educated.
Explains the link between dignity, self-respect, and happiness.
Writing is in paragraph form with supporting examples.
Response moves beyond restating the poster — shows independent thinking.

items.item_stem: Choose ONE of the following projects and complete it. Project A: Research two government schemes launched in India for the education of the girl child (you may look up schemes such as Beti Bachao Beti Padhao or Balika Samridhi Yojana). For each scheme, note its name, its main goal, and one way it has helped girls attend school. Present your findings in a short written note of six to eight sentences. Project B: India is a multilingual country. Make a survey of the languages spoken by people around you — family members, neighbours, or classmates. List at least five languages, note how many people speak each, and write three sentences explaining why you think this linguistic diversity is a strength for India.

expected_elements: Project A: two schemes correctly named with their goals stated.
Project A: at least one concrete benefit for girl child education noted per scheme.
Project B: a clear list of at least five languages with counts.
Project B: three sentences linking multilingualism to national strength.
Either project: writing is organised, factually grounded, and in the student's own words.
